summary: ORION is a mobile farm management platform that helps small farmers in Nicaragua adapt to erratic rainfall, heat and soil degradation by combining field sensors with NASA Earth observation data. It addresses Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data by turning climate science into plot-level guidance. Farmers outline their land with GPS or on a map, divide it into plots, register crops and link a solar-powered ESP32 sensor node that measures soil water tension, soil temperature, air temperature and humidity, rainfall and standing water. These readings are paired with NASA POWER daily climate and soil wetness, GPM IMERG satellite rainfall and SMAP soil moisture, so each plot has both a field-level and a regional view. ORION translates the data into simple color-coded alerts for storms, heavy rain, drought, frost and fungal risk, an activity calendar, crop growth stages, audio narration and an AI assistant, and compares crop rotation options using climate, water, drainage and planting history. Our test farm in Sébaco, Matagalpa, already uses 45 days of real NASA POWER data, and the app, database and server foundation is built and tested. Sensor firmware, live NASA synchronization and field validation with farmers and agronomists are the next steps. With local calibration, the approach could serve smallholder farms across Central America.
details:
ORION is a mobile farm management platform that connects what happens in a farmer’s field with what NASA satellites observe from space. Developed for Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data, it focuses on small and medium producers in Nicaragua, where irregular rainfall, heat, waterlogging and soil degradation make planting and crop management increasingly uncertain. Many of these farmers have no tools that relate the conditions of their own plots to climate information.

Farmers map their land by walking its boundary with the phone’s GPS or by placing points on a map, then divide it into plots and register each crop with its planting date. In the field, a solar-powered node built around an ESP32 microcontroller reads WATERMARK soil water tension sensors, a DS18B20 soil temperature probe, an SHT31-D air temperature and humidity sensor, a rain gauge and float switches that detect standing water, sending readings every 15 minutes. On the server, these measurements are paired with NASA POWER daily temperature, precipitation, humidity, radiation, wind and soil wetness, GPM IMERG satellite rainfall and SMAP regional soil moisture, all linked to the plot’s coordinates. Each record keeps its source, unit and timestamp, so direct measurements are never confused with satellite estimates.

The app translates this information into color-coded alerts with plain-language messages, crop growth stages, an agricultural calendar, audio narration and an AI assistant that answers questions in Nicaraguan Spanish. Alert thresholds are defined in code: fungal risk when humidity stays above 90% for six hours between 15 and 25 °C, heavy rain above 25 mm per day, drought after seven days with under 2 mm of rain and low NASA soil wetness, and frost warnings only for farms above 900 m. A rotation module compares crop alternatives using temperature, water availability, season, crop history, drainage and soil conservation, following FAO conservation agriculture principles. Its creative contribution is joining a farmer’s own map, live field sensors and NASA data in a single, accessible view.

The mobile app is built with React Native and Expo in TypeScript, using Expo Router, MapLibre for maps, TanStack Query with an offline cache, Victory Native for charts and Expo Speech for narration and voice input. The backend runs on Supabase, with PostgreSQL and PostGIS for farm geometry, phone-number login, storage and Deno Edge Functions for sensor ingestion, NASA synchronization, alerts and rotation analysis. A pnpm and Turborepo monorepo holds shared packages for the design system, Zod-validated data types, translations and core logic, with continuous integration on GitHub Actions.

Our test farm in Sébaco, Matagalpa, uses 45 days of real NASA POWER data from October 1 to November 14, 2026, showing 304.7 mm of rain over 37 rainy days and an average humidity of 87%. Those are conditions that raise fungal risk. The software foundation includes 25 database tables with row-level security, 20 server functions, 26 app routes and about 100 automated tests, all passing. We also produced app wireframes, a clickable prototype, a sensor wiring diagram, architecture and sequence diagrams and a 3D model of the farm installation. The sensor firmware, live NASA synchronization and full app screens are still in development.

The team considered sensor cost and weather protection, solar energy autonomy, the difference between SMAP’s coarse grid and small plots, the fact that IMERG provides observed estimates rather than forecasts, missing NASA values and unreliable rural connectivity. These considerations led to an offline-first design. SMAP reports volumetric water content while WATERMARK measures soil water tension, so ORION presents them as complementary views rather than comparing them directly. Mentor feedback on sensor selection and costs for small farmers shaped the hardware design.

ORION is designed for small farmers, agricultural technicians, cooperatives and students. Our intended impact is to help farmers detect problems early, plan irrigation, drainage and planting with better information, and choose rotations that protect their soil. Field tests with farmers and agronomists are the next step to validate the alerts and rotation guidance, after which the approach could be adapted to other crops and regions across Central America.
